title: Eating out
goal: Order food, name flavors, ask for more, pay — and understand why "have you eaten?" is the most important question in the Philippines.
bekal: asking for more rice, broth and a spoon without awkwardness
responding to an invitation to eat the right way

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sa karinderya
dialogs.intro: A simple roadside eatery. Dishes line up behind glass, and customers point at what they want.

lines.speaker: Tindera:
lines.text: Sir, ano po ang ulam ninyo?
lines.id: Sir, what dish would you like?
lines.literal: sir, what ma'am the dish your-all?

lines.speaker: Tindera:
lines.text: Bagong luto ang adobo at ang sinigang na baboy.
lines.id: The adobo and the pork sinigang are freshly cooked.
lines.literal: newly cooked the adobo and the sinigang that pork.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sinigang na lang po. Isang kanin din po.
lines.id: Just the sinigang, please. And one rice too.
lines.literal: sinigang now just ma'am. one rice also ma'am.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dito na lang po. May tubig po ba?
lines.literal: here now just ma'am. there's water ma'am Q?

lines.speaker: Budi:

lines.id: Thank you. Could I also have a spoon?

lines.speaker: Tindera:
lines.id: Here you go. Enjoy your meal!

lines.text: Sarap! Puwede po bang dagdagan ng kanin?

notes: **A karinderya is a people's eatery**: dishes cooked since morning line up behind glass and you simply point. Think of a cafeteria-style lunch counter. Another word for this kind of place: *turo-turo*, literally "point-point" — from how you order.

**Ulam is a word worth understanding properly.** It means the dish eaten with rice — anything served alongside it. Filipinos don't consider a meal complete without rice, so *ano ang ulam?* really asks "what are we having with our rice today?".

**Kanin is cooked rice**, *bigas* is raw rice, and *palay* is rice in the paddy. Three words for one thing at three stages — English has just "rice" for all of them. (Malay and Indonesian share this kind of split, a clear sign the languages are related.)

**Kain po kayo!** is an invitation you'll hear everywhere, even from strangers eating next to you. It's sincere hospitality but also etiquette: the polite reply is *Salamat po, kumain na po ako* if you don't want to join.
**Dagdagan ng kanin** uses receiver focus from unit 13: what gets added to is your plate. A shorter form that's also common: *Extra rice po.*
**Unlimited rice** is an institution in the Philippines — many eateries offer endless rice, and that's where the English phrase is used as is, with no translation.
**Sarap!** is the short form of *ang sarap!* and works as a compliment on its own. Praising the cooking out loud in the Philippines isn't excessive, it's expected.
**Libre means free** (from Spanish *libre*). It's also used for treating someone: *Libre kita* — "my treat". One of the offers you'll hear most from Filipino friends.
**Dine-in or take-out** — two English terms used even in the tiniest eatery. Tagalog equivalents exist (*dito kakainin* / *iuuwi*), but they're rarely used.

grammars.title: Ordering: the pattern that always works
body: Orders in the Philippines nearly always take the form: number + linker + food + *po*. No verb needed at all.
after: The first pattern is enough for your whole life in the Philippines. If you only memorize one sentence from this unit, make it *Isang … po.*
To ask for the check: *Bill out po* or *Ang bill po*. To ask for a takeaway box: *Pa-take-out po*.
For a dish whose name you don't know, just point and say *Iyan po* — "that one". Nobody considers it rude at a karinderya.

grammars.title: Flavors and the state of food
body: All the flavor words use the *ma-* prefix you know from unit 3.
after: Look at *maalat* and *maasim* — close cousins of Malay/Indonesian *asin* and *asam* (salty, sour), with the letters shifted slightly.
The exclamation form drops *ma-*: *Ang sarap!*, *Ang anghang!*, *Ang tamis!* This is what you'll say most at the table.
To decline politely, use *hindi masyado*: *Hindi masyadong maanghang para sa akin* — "not very spicy for me" or "too spicy for me", depending on tone.

blocks.title: If you don't eat pork
items: Say so from the start: *Hindi po ako kumakain ng baboy.* — "I don't eat pork." It's understood at once and respected, not least because the Philippines has a large Muslim population in the south.

Look for **manok** (chicken), **isda** (fish), **baka** (beef) and **gulay** (vegetables) on the dish list. Avoid **baboy** (pork), **lechon**, **sisig**, **chicharon** and **bagoong**, which often contain pork or shrimp.
Halal restaurants exist in many cities; look for a *halal* sign or ask *May halal po ba dito?*

blocks.text: The main utensils in the Philippines are a **spoon and fork** — knives rarely appear on a home table, since dishes are cut small in the kitchen. Eating with your hands (*kamayan*) is also common and seen as special, especially at shared feasts spread on banana leaves (*boodle fight*).

items: Could I have a spoon, please?
